q: It’s behavior that isn’t dangerous or threatening, and therefore doesn’t rise to the level of involving an administrator.
The key to handling brazen behavior is to control your desire to rush in, show your displeasure, and put them in their place.
Your students will be expecting you to act shocked and angry, like most adults in similar situations. You must do the opposite.
Keeping it a mystery from the rest of the class sends a stronger message that such behavior is unacceptable.
Just review what they did, remind them of the addendum, and tell them what the consequence will be. Do not lecture or tell them what to think or how they should feel.
Brazenness shows a clear lack of respect for you, for learning, and for their fellow classmates. It will grow and spread unless you handle it with the shrewd craftiness it deserves.

t: The Trait Every Great Teacher Shares
q: It’s something lasting, highly influential, and part of who the teacher is. It’s woven into their manner and demeanor.
You see, teachers who are uncertain or dubious about their classroom management approach always struggle.
Students know fear and weakness in their teacher when they see it, even if it lies below the surface. They can smell it from across the playground.
You can be confident and surefooted outside of the classroom and find yourself perplexed and struggling for air within it. Teaching can be especially unforgiving in this way.
You’re better off embracing one methodology than following your own hybrid system or an approach you don’t fully understand.
Which puts them at ease, removes their excitability, and frees them to settle down, settle in, and focus on learning.
